rootbridges/hook: In the rainy hills of [Meghalaya](/mˌɛɡɐlˈeɪə/), in India, there are bridges that are alive.
rootbridges/grow: Villagers guide the roots of rubber fig trees across the river, using bamboo and hollow trunks to hold them.
rootbridges/slow: It takes about fifteen years before a bridge is strong enough to walk on.
rootbridges/strong: And unlike steel, it gets stronger as the roots keep thickening, so some can last for hundreds of years.
rootbridges/long: One of the longest is about fifty three metres across.
rootbridges/unesco: Their villages were added to India's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage in twenty twenty two.
rootbridges/end: You don't build this bridge once. You grow it, and the next generation inherits it.
roopkund/hook: High in the Indian Himalayas, a frozen lake is surrounded by human skeletons.
roopkund/where: Roopkund Lake sits at about five thousand metres, and its bones were left in the ice and snow.
roopkund/old: For years, people assumed everyone died together in one disaster, around eight hundred A.D.
roopkund/dna: In twenty nineteen, scientists studied the DNA of thirty eight of the skeletons, and found they were not one group.
roopkund/south: Most had South Asian ancestry, but they died at different times, in more than one event.
roopkund/med: Another fourteen had Mediterranean ancestry, and died about a thousand years later.
roopkund/end: Why were Mediterranean travellers in the Himalayas? The study could not say.
botodolphin/hook: In the Amazon, there is a dolphin that turns pink.
botodolphin/born: Amazon river dolphins are born grey, and slowly turn pink as they grow.
botodolphin/male: Males tend to be pinker than females, and scientists link this to scars from fights.
botodolphin/neck: Their neck bones are not fused like most dolphins, so they can bend and turn their heads easily.
botodolphin/flood: When the rains flood the forest, they swim between the trees.
botodolphin/size: It is the largest river dolphin species in the world.
botodolphin/end: But fishing and pollution put them at risk, and scientists are still working out how many remain.
lencois/hook: This looks like a desert in Brazil. But it gets far more rain than a real desert.
lencois/dunes: [Lençóis Maranhenses](/lɛnsˈɔɪs mˌɛɹɐnjˈɛnsɪs/) has endless white dunes, some about forty metres high.
lencois/lagoons: Between January and June, rain fills the valleys between the dunes, and thousands of blue lagoons appear.
lencois/why: A layer of hard, waterproof sediment under the sand stops the water from draining away.
lencois/fish: Fish arrive with the water, and some survive the dry season by sleeping in the mud.
lencois/unesco: In twenty twenty four, the park became a UNESCO World Heritage site.
lencois/end: A desert that floods. Would you swim in it?
krakatoa/hook: In eighteen eighty three, a volcano in Indonesia made the loudest sound in modern history.
krakatoa/sound: People heard it nearly five thousand kilometres away, and its pressure wave circled the Earth more than three times.
krakatoa/waves: Huge tsunamis struck the nearby coasts, and over thirty thousand people died, mostly from the waves.
krakatoa/sky: Ash and gas in the upper air painted vivid red sunsets around the world for months.
krakatoa/cool: Global temperatures dipped, and took about five years to return to normal.
krakatoa/child: Today, a new volcano called [Anak Krakatau](/ˈɑːnɑːk kɹˌɑːkɐtˈaʊ/), the Child of Krakatoa, rises where it once stood.
krakatoa/end: A reminder that the ground beneath the sea is still alive.
kawahijen/hook: Deep inside a volcano in Indonesia, a river of fire glows electric blue.
kawahijen/not: It is not lava. It is sulfur gas, burning when it meets the air.
kawahijen/flow: Some of the sulfur condenses into liquid, which burns and flows like blue lava.
kawahijen/lake: Next to it lies a turquoise crater lake, one of the most acidic in the world.
kawahijen/miners: Miners climb down into the crater, often at night, to collect the yellow sulfur.
kawahijen/risk: The fumes are hard on the lungs, and the work is dangerous.
kawahijen/end: Beauty and hard labour, side by side, inside one crater.
naica/hook: Nearly three hundred metres under a Mexican desert, there is a cave of giant crystals.
naica/size: Some of the crystals are over eleven metres long, among the largest natural crystals ever found.
naica/what: They are selenite, a form of gypsum, grown slowly in hot, mineral rich water.
naica/heat: But the air is about fifty eight degrees Celsius, and extremely humid.
naica/suit: Without special cooling gear, a person can survive there only a short time.
naica/flood: The mine closed in twenty fifteen because of flooding, and the cave is hard to reach today.
naica/end: A hidden world, grown in the dark, and sealed away again.
axolotl/hook: This smiling animal can grow back its own limbs.
axolotl/where: It is the axolotl, and in the wild it lives only around [Xochimilco](/ˌsoʊtʃɪmˈɪlkoʊ/), near Mexico City.
axolotl/baby: Unlike most salamanders, it keeps its baby features, like feathery gills, for life.
axolotl/regrow: It can regrow limbs, organs, and even parts of its brain.
axolotl/science: That is why scientists study them, hoping to learn more about healing.
axolotl/wild: In the wild, they are critically endangered, with fewer than a thousand estimated to remain.
axolotl/end: Polluted canals and invasive fish hurt them. Thousands live in tanks, but wild ones need help.
